utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton; intern, Agnieszka Bugaj; and case manager, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Chris Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in. Closed session, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ma'am, you have protective measures, pseudonym and voice distortion and face distortion -- no voice. Okay, face distortion. Pseudonym and face distortion. Therefore, we won't mention your name and we will address you as "Witness," simply as "Witness." You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you now read the solemn declaration the usher will give you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your witness, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I ask the court usher to please show the witness 65 ter 06382, not to be broadcast. And this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For the personal data of the witness, wouldn't it be better to go into private session, Ms. Clanton?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Because you will probably ask some questions about her career and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is simply the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I know, but afterwards, wouldn't you ask some questions that would better be asked in private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to not do that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So pseudonym sheet, not broadcast. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, the Court has ordered certain protective measures with respect to you and your evidence, including a pseudonym and image distortion. If you could please look at the pseudonym sheet that appears in front of you. Without reading anything on the sheet in front of you, can you tell us if it is your name that appears.

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And directing your attention to where it says "date of birth," is that your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the pseudonym sheet, 06382, into evidence under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1018. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Can I ask the court officer to please bring up 65 ter number 02389 at this time, not to be broadcast. I would also like to ask the usher to provide a hard copy to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Witness, did you give a statement to representatives of the ICTY in June 1999 in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise this as your statement?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If you could please look at your screen at the English version in front of you and tell me if you recognise the signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And before testifying today, did you have a chance to review a translation of this statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And for the next question I'd like to go into closed session, please -- private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, with the corrections that you've just indicated, are you satisfied that the information contained in your written statement is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And again, with the corrections we have just made, if you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And finally, now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and the truthfulness of your statement?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would like to tender 65 ter 2389 and the associated exhibit 2388 into evidence under seal. We've also prepared the redacted version of the statement, which is 65 ter 02389.1, which may also be admitted. The associated exhibit is at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The confidential statement shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1019, admitted under seal. The public redacted version of the statement shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1019.1. And the associated exhibit, 65 ter document 2388 shall be Exhibit Number 1020. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the associated exhibit should also be admitted under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we do that, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, if you feel that answering any question would reveal your identity, you may indicate your concerns about answering that question publicly, that is, in open session. Before the war began, what was the ethnic composition of Klisa?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: 10 per cent Croat, 90 per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how far from Klisa is the town of Celije?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I would not know now exactly how many kilometres, but it's not far by road.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What happened in Celije in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: We saw thick smoke, a lot of smoke, and we knew something terrible had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of Celije?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: It was 100 per cent Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What happened to the Croats of Celije?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Some were killed and some managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What impact did this destruction of Celije have on you and the local Croat population in Klisa?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: That caused great fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in Klisa in 1991, were there any changes that you observed in respect of the people who you saw in the village?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: When the troops started coming in, our local people changed completely. It was not the same population as before.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: These troops that came in, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What information did you hear about where they came from?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: It was said they came from Belgrade, Kragujevac, Nis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: A variety of uniforms because there were all sorts of troops, the Yugoslav People's Army and those paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And a moment ago you mentioned the Serbs who were from Klisa. How were these local Serbs dressing at this time?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: The men wore those military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Did you hear that the local Serbs who wore the military uniforms belonged to or were linked with any armed units in the area?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes, because they were all together. They went around together. They drove around in cars together.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Have you heard of Arkan and his men or Arkan and his volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Did you hear that the local Serbs in uniform had any connections with these units?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What did you hear in the village about who the local Serbs were associated with?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection. The -- actually, the witness's potential answer has now been contaminated by the leading question, hasn't it? So I object --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can ask the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I object to both the questions and I would suggest that even a neutral answer [sic] now is going to contaminate the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Witness, what did you observe about the behaviour of these local Serbs and Serbs who had just come to the region?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Where were they meeting?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Well, they got together and some moved into the houses of Croats who had left, and others had a building that used to be a co-operative or a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you know if they went to any other towns?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Well, they drove around everywhere. They did not really walk about. They drove around, but where they went I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the towns where they went?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Those Serbian villages around -- between us and Vukovar, so they probably went to those Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Can you provide us with any names?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Tenja.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask that 65 ter 06373, a photograph, be placed in front of the witness. This is at tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you recognise the road and the building in this picture?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the road?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: It's Vukovarska Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what town is this in?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Klisa.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And the gate and the building that are visible on the left side, do you recognise those buildings?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I can't see any buildings depicted in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you see the gate?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you know who owns the property that is behind the gate?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the exhibit is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1021. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I think we need to go back into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Mr. Gosnell, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings and I have just a very few questions for you today. If any of my questions aren't clear, please feel free to ask me to elaborate or clarify. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 00978, please. And this was on tab 7 of the OTP's original exhibit list. And I'm interested, in particular, in zooming in on the paragraph immediately after the first full subheading, and that subheading reads: "The arming of the Serbs, barricades." And that's on page 2 of the English at the very top of the page, and in the B/C/S it should be down there starting at the bottom of the left-hand column. Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, I just want to ask you about some details surrounding what was going in Klisa before this event that you've been talking about today. And here it says that: "Klisa village, next to the Osijek airport, is a village with 12 Croatian and more than 100 Serbian houses. Even though in Trpinja - the neighbouring village is, just like Klisa, on the road to Vukovar - barricades were set up as early as in May, the Serbs from Klisa delayed setting them up until 24 August." Now, as far as you can recall, is that correct, that barricades were not set up in Klisa until the 24th of August?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I really can't remember any of the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And there's an individual who is reported as having made a statement in this article and it's someone named Josip Horvat. Do you know Josip Horvat?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He is reported here as saying at some point that I saw -- and I quote: "'I saw that the Serbs were arming themselves and where they unloaded and stored automatic weapons. When I told this to our Guards at the airport, they replied several days later that they had received an order from Osijek that they must not disarm the Serbs ...'" Now, what I want to ask you about this is whether you know whether there were Guards present at the Osijek airport at any time, May, June, July, August 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were Guards or any armed Croatian forces at all anywhere in the area of Klisa, in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: In Klisa, the only armed people were the Serb army. I don't know about anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when is it that the Serb army arrived there?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Sometime after Celije. Celije was set on fire and then things started happening gradually. I really don't know when that happened in Celije.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, a little bit further down in this article it says: "Three days after the barricades were set up in Klisa, the Yugoslav Army began to arrive with tanks, personnel carriers, guns, and mortars. And on the fifth day, there were more than 700 reservists in the village." Now, you've already testified about the arrival of the JNA, but in terms of numbers, do you have any idea whether that's -- that number would be correct, approximately? Were there 700 reservists in the village by that time?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The village was full of troops. I couldn't believe my eyes when I saw so many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have P311, please, which is tab 3 of the Prosecution's original list. I didn't expect that marking to be there. That's not on the version of P311 that I have. In any event, I don't think it's important, but perhaps we could zoom in somewhat on the area around the -- what's marked there as the Osijek airport. Just a little bit, maybe one click, maybe one more. That's perfect. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, here on this map we do see Klisa. And is that an accurate representation of where Klisa is --

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you help us understand, to the best of your recollection, after the arrival of the JNA troops, where was the -- if there was at all, where was the boundary line approximately between where the Serb forces were and where the Croat forces were? Can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Osijek, near Nemetin, this is where the Croats were. Tenja was in the Serb hands, Klisa as well, Bobota, Pacetin, Bijelo Brdo -- now you have moved the map. Can you leave it like this? Thank you. Serbs held Klisa, Vera, Bobota, Trpinja, Silas. They burned down Celije. Laslovo was also occupied. Please slow down, don't move the map so fast. Antunovac was a Croatian village, it was occupied. Tenja was a Serb village. Antunovac was a Croatian village but occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, if I could just assist. I think there's a problem with the screen because it seems to be focusing in when you touch the screen. So perhaps what we can do is zoom back out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the Registrar can help and just zoom in a little bit more up in the top half of the document -- yes, that's perfect. Let's just leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, ma'am, if you could just describe that again but this time without touching the screen in front of you, it will be easier.

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: The Serb army occupied Tenja. Klisa was occupied. Vera was a purely Serb village. I can't see Bobota here, it's on the other side, but I'm not touching anything. Antunovac was a Croatian village, people fled from it. And then Bijelo Brdo was a predominantly Serb village. People fled from Sarvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So at this time was Tenja within Serb territory or was it in Croat territory?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: It was Croatian territory; however, it was occupied by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you mean by that that there was some kind of a boundary between Klisa and Tenja where there were opposing Serb and Croat forces but that --

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps you could explain that a little further because I'm not sure that I understand.

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. The Serbs occupied Tenja. Klisa was also occupied, and they co-operated, Serbs from Tenja and Serbs from Klisa, Vera, Bobota, Silas, and all the other surrounding places, they co-operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that at this time, in October/November 1991, that Serb forces held Tenja?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: It was occupied. Tenja was under the Serb occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you know whether there was any infiltration by Croatian forces through that front line, through -- into the area that was held by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were asked the question by the Prosecutor whether your husband was co-operating with or procured supplies for Croat forces, and you said the answer to that was no. Do you know whether there was anyone in Klisa village who was assisting Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody in Klisa had any weapons or any assistance. We were a minority there. There were just a few Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, about the map, the unmarked version of this map is, as the Registrar kindly told me, 65 ter number 6329. Wouldn't it be appropriate to have that one -- I don't know if we still need it on the screen, but that we -- that you would tender this one rather than work on a marked version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think that's quite a good idea, Mr. President. In fact, in order to make the record absolutely clear, it's been described well, but nonetheless, to make the record clear I think I'd like to bring up 06329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in to approximately where we had the zoom with the other map. I think that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could I kindly ask you, with the assistance of the usher, to take a pen and mark on the map where it is that there was the limit between Serb forces and Croat forces in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I could not know exactly. I wasn't there. All I know is that they entered Osijek. How far, though, I don't know. They entered Osijek, but how far they went in depth I wouldn't know. I know they held Tenja, the Serbs, but in the territory between Osijek and Tenja, how far they went I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, instead of having you mark specifically, because it seems that you don't know -- you don't have the answer to the question with that level of precision, so let's not have you mark, but let me just ask you a couple of more specific questions. You've already said that Antunovac -- you said that according to your information, according to what you know -- knew, Antunovac in November 1991 was in Croat hands; correct?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when Antunovac was occupied. I know it was occupied, but I can't tell you the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in the fall of 1991, leaving aside any precise or specific date, was Antunovac in Croat hands?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: I don't know the dates. I can't tell you. It developed in such a way that I know they occupied it, but I can't you when. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Witness, who do you refer to when you say "they occupied"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm done with that map. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And I won't tender it in any fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Madam Witness, you mention in your witness statement at page 1 of the English -- at page 2 of the English and at page 3 of the English, a certain Rajko Mizdrak, and he's mentioned several times. And last night we received information from the Prosecution that on the basis of their conversations with you, they understood that Rajko Mizdrak was training at Arkan's training centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GH-107
utterances.text: There was talk about that. People said that. I wasn't there to see it, but people said that's true.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, could you repeat that for the public record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Madam Witness, thank you very much for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Witness, this brings your testimony to an end. Thank you for coming to assist the Tribunal with your testimony. You are now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey back home. The court usher will escort you out of court in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to suggest that the next witness is ready. It involves a bit of a personnel change within the team, and it's possible we could take the break a few minutes early and come back after the break, then, and be all situated for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Stringer, we have to take the break for the voice distortion that this witness has. So we'll take the break and come back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There is one matter that we wish to raise before the next witness is brought in. If we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, as you have protective measures, we will refer to you as -- simply as "Witness" or "Mr. Witness," just to avoid mentioning your name. You should also be aware of the shielding of your identity while in open session, and whenever you need to say something that could reveal your identity, you can just indicate to us that we have to go into private session. Now, you are going to read the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give untruthful or misleading information to the Tribunal. Can I now ask you to read the solemn declaration the usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, President, Your Honours. Could we please get 65 ter document 6380 on the screen but not publicly broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, do you see your name and date of birth on the sheet in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we admit that into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1022, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get 65 ter document 3258 on the screen, please. And at this point, could I ask for some assistance to hand the witness a hard copy of his statement as we proceed through it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Looking at the statement, sir, do you recognise this -- sorry, firstly, did you give a statement to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in May 2012?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recognise this to be the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were you given the opportunity to read the statement in your own language before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And this week in The Hague, have you again been given the opportunity to read your statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, I understand there are some corrections to be made to the statement and I'm going to go through those. Firstly, at paragraph 18, the last sentence refers to as many as 4.000 shells hitting Vukovar Hospital per day. And I understand that this figure is too high. So my question is: What would you like to say about the intensity of the shelling of the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Well, a couple of thousand fell daily, up to 2.000. I made a little mistake there because when I read I was not able to see whether it was my mistake or the interpreter's mistake, but it was not 4.000. It was up to 2.000 a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I ask you to talk slowly so as to give the interpreters the opportunity to follow correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Next, is it correct that at paragraph 19 of your statement you wanted to remove the terms "the warehouse" so that the sentence would read: "Those who had received medical assistance, they were moved to the nuclear shelter in Borovo Komerc to make room for new patients."

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was a technical error. It should have read "shelter," not "warehouse." I only noticed when I re-read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Next, in relation to paragraph 30, I understand you wanted to correct the reference to Captain Sasa arriving with two Chetniks called Nedjeljko Vojnovic and Bogdan Kuzmic. Is it correct that there were two Chetniks with Captain Sasa in addition to Nedjeljko Vojnovic and Bogdan Kuzmic?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: There were two Chetniks together with Captain Sasa. And this Vojnovic and - what's the name of the other one? - Kuzmic, they were employees of the hospital, except that Kuzmic was wearing a uniform because already in June or July he had left the hospital and was no longer working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than that, are there any more changes that need to be made to the statement?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of the statement?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you were asked about these same matters today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we tender the 65 ter statement 3258. We also have a public redacted version, 3258.1, that we would tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Gillett, there is kind of a problem with the annex to the statement which are a series of photographs marked by the witness, and they're uploaded in e-court in black and white. Markings almost invisible. We were wondering whether you have the coloured version available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: As always, you've predicted the next topic. Indeed, these are the associated exhibits, and as you observed, the copies that came out were in black and white. We've also -- have the originals that he marked in a previous case in colour that we included on the exhibit list, and we've included an additional list that we made, which is 03258.2, which links each of the coloured versions that he originally marked in previous proceedings with each of the pages of the black and white photos that were annexed to his current statement so that you can easily tell which one is which. So we would ask that they're all admitted for the interests of simplicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And you're sure that now on your exhibit list there is a coloured version of these photographs? Because when we looked into it, there was a black and white version of the photos in it with no markings at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: There should indeed be a colour version. And, for example, if we went to 65 ter 02620, I believe that that will be a colour version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen just to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I believe the markings are clearer to see on this version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. The statement is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The confidential statement shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1023, and the public redacted version shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1023.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I understand that in the usual procedure, with the court officer we'll address the associated exhibits. And if there's any more information required about the coloured versions of the photos, we can provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, turning to the substance of your statement, I'm going to ask you some additional questions about the shelling of Vukovar. Firstly, at paragraph 10 of the statement you say that in August 1991, the JNA shelled civilian targets in Vukovar and that your apartment was hit. Aside from your apartment, what other civilian locations were hit at this time?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: That was a settlement of four-storey and two-storey buildings. They bombed that from the air. My building was hit and the building facing mine, that one burnt down almost completely; and at the other end of the street another building was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you given any form of warning before these shells hit your building and the buildings around it?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: No, we had no warning and we were not expecting it because they were targeting only military installations or those of strategic importance, the silo, the castle, and the secondary school because that's where the members of the Croatian Home Guard were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In your statement you say prior to this shelling in mid-August, they had been targeting military locations and that this was the first targeting of civilian locations. And my question, to clarify: Why did you not expect a warning before there would be shelling of civilian locations?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: We were not expecting it. We thought they would not target civilian buildings, but that started at Mitnica itself. They started targeting civilian buildings in Mitnica and then all over the town. We were really unprepared. We thought they would not target civilians. We thought they would only concentrate on the location where the members of the Croatian Home Guards Corps were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And during the attack on Vukovar, while it was being shelled, did the inhabitants try to flee the city?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Some tried, but it was difficult. You see, we were encircled. All around Vukovar were Serbian villages and there were roadblocks and barricades there. It was almost impossible to leave Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 26 and the preceding paragraphs, you described the JNA and paramilitaries arriving at the Vukovar Hospital, and specifically at paragraph 26 you describe realising that you were going to have to leave Vukovar and being upset. Now, why did you have to leave the city in which you had grown up?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: can go where they want to, to Croatia or Serbia. I was very sorry to even contemplate leaving my town because I grew up there, I lived there all my life, and I was very sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can we get a redaction at page 37, line 5 to 6, about the supervisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you mentioned you were sorry to have to leave the town of Vukovar, but why did you have to leave the town of Vukovar? Why couldn't you stay there?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: We were told that nobody could stay, only Serbs could stay, employees of the hospital of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who did this message come from or who was telling you you were no longer allowed to stay in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who is Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Major. Veselin Sljivancanin, major, I think, by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning again to your description of the JNA and military -- paramilitaries arriving at the hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could we go into private session for this next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Moving to paragraph 47 of your statement, in this paragraph you mention that while you were on the bus at the JNA barracks and while this threatening behaviour was occurring, one local Chetnik said that: "The ones that Neso had put on the list cannot be saved. Things will not end well for them." What did he mean that things would not end up well for these people?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Well, that they would kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how did he know this, that they would kill them?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: You know, I suppose that all those who were in the barracks, those paramilitaries, they all knew what would happen. I can't be sure of that, but that's what I assume and eventually that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And to clarify, when you say "would kill them" and "that's what would happen," which killing are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean? What are you asking me? For example, when we saw that list -- and I will -- I believe that we will come back to that later. When we were on our way back to the hospital, they had already killed one of the hospital staff, a man who had worked in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What I'm asking, to clarify, is when you mentioned they would kill them, I'm asking -- and you said that this is what happened, where were the victims killed, aside from this one individual, I'm talking about the group.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: That person was killed in the hospital, Ivan Bozak. We already said that. He was killed in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, not the individual, but all the other people, where were they killed?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: At Ovcara. They were taken from the barracks to Ovcara. They were all executed there. Perhaps only five or six managed to save themselves. I know some of their names, I can tell you who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It's okay for the meanwhile. Now, during proofing yesterday you were shown a video and I'm going to ask you some questions about some parts of that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get video 04892 on the screen. And the first clip is going to be at 0 minutes and 43 seconds through to 0 minutes and 47 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the people in this shot?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I recognise Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now go to 51 minutes, 54 seconds, to 51 minutes and 59 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can we pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in this picture?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I recognise a few of them. Those were all civilians from the Mitnica. I also lived there which is why I know all of them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what are they doing?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: They are walking to a collection centre, as far as I know. Pilip Karaula was its commander and the other one was Zdravko Komsic. They negotiated with the international community - I suppose that the guy, the blond guy, that was standing next to the community [as interpreted], came from the international community - and with the army and they agreed a surrender. And all the civilians from the Mitnica were to be protected. They are now walking to a collection centre and from there they were all transferred to Mitrovica. I even saw them leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could now play clip 52 minutes and 12 seconds through to 53 minutes and 18 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I have nothing left. But please be honest with me! Tell me honestly, don't say the things that are not true. Tell me only the truth. "We are innocent. "What are the conditions like in the town? "[In English] The town is totally broken. We have nothing. The houses are burned ... the hospital ... we did not have for three months, no food, no water, no medical things. They have killed all our friends and we are not guilty. We didn't want the war, we only love people. We don't kill them and we still don't hate. We still don't hate. "[Interpretation] My heart is broken."

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The conditions in Vukovar that this girl describes, including the lack of medical supplies and the lack of food, is that consistent with what you experienced in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Precisely so. At the hospital we had some supplies, but those who were hiding in the basements of private houses, they had very little food. Guard members supplied us with pigs and cows that roamed the streets of the city, but there was no water. We could not kill them and skin them in a very safe way. But the hospital had experts who examined the meat, so we had food. We didn't have bread, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now go to 1 hour, 11 minutes, and 15 seconds, and play the clip through to 1 hour, 11 minutes, and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in this shot?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: This is our doctor, our dentist, and her father.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what are these people doing?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: These people are in the centre of Vukovar. They lived there. And over bullhorns they were informed to go to the Velepromet collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why were they told to go to the Velepromet collection centre?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Well, I really wouldn't know that. That's how things were decided. The men were separated from the women and from the Serb citizens. They separated the Serbs and they set them free, whereas people of Croatian ethnicity and other ethnicities were treated differently. The men were separated from the women. And you will see later that the men were then sent to some hangars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now go to the clip 1 hour and 12 minutes and 36 seconds, through to 1 hour, 13 minutes, and 0 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Who are these soldiers? How would you describe them?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I would say that they were paramilitaries because they were not completely clad in uniforms. JNA soldiers had different uniforms. Their uniforms were complete. They were neat, clean-shaven. They looked like the real army, and here in the clip you can see that their uniforms are not complete. One part of their uniform was of one kind and the other part of the uniform was of a different kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now go to clip 1 hour, 22 minutes, and 25 seconds, to 1 hour, 22 minutes, and 37 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: with this company. They were wholesalers, and I was in the warehouse and in this courtyard at least once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can I get a redaction of the line 23 to 24 , where he states his position, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And we're going to now turn to the final part of this video which is the final exhibit I'm dealing with here. If we could go to clip 1 hour, 39 minutes, and 24 seconds, through to 1 hour, 39 minutes, and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: First, what building is this?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: This is the hospital. This is the main entrance to the new block.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what are all the people doing outside?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: These are civilians. When Vukovar fell, civilians came from all over the place and arrived at the hospital because they thought they would be safe there, that nobody would touch them if they were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did that turn out to be correct, that they would be safe and untouched at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Well, it was correct; however, the agreement with the JNA and the Red Cross from Vukovar was that they would come to fetch them and transport them. A list of all those who were there and who were loaded onto the trucks and taken to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now play clip 1 hour, 53 minutes and 47 seconds, through to 1 hour and 54 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What are these two rooms that were shown?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: That was the only true atomic shelter in the hospital. It consisted of two separate rooms and that's where infants were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could you describe briefly the conditions at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: The conditions were terrible. When that shell hit the hospital, it shattered all the window-panes on the -- all the new hospital buildings. All the patients had to be lowered into the basement because there were no conditions for them to stay on any of the floors. It was terrible. The shell fell and the detonation was so strong that it shattered all the window-panes. It destroyed all the doors and windows. The patients could not be guaranteed safety, which is why they had to be lowered to the lower floors in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would now tender this video 4892 for admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1024. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And that concludes my questions on direct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. My name is Zoran Zivanovic and I represent Goran Hadzic in these proceedings. I have a few questions for you that arise from your statement and your testimony so far. First of all, I wanted to ask you, or rather, I would like to shed some more light on the things that you have spoken about here today. On page 32, you said that about 2.000 shells a day fell on the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether you're sure about the figure?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I can't be sure. Nobody can be sure. I know that from early morning, from 7.00 until 11.00, that one shell hit the hospital every minute and that's how I made my calculations. If you calculate the number of hours -- although the shells fell even during the night but not so many. The shelling was constant; it just didn't stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to my rough estimate, that would mean that there was one shell every half a minute?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Approximately so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone and could the counsel be instructed to switch off his mike when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness and Mr. Zivanovic, two things. You both should, as you speak the same language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As you both speak the same language and in order to assist the interpreters, you should stop after question and before answering, so as to allow the interpreters to follow. Second, Mr. Zivanovic -- and the witness could eventually be attentive to that too. Mr. Zivanovic's microphone has to be shut off before you start answering because through that microphone there is no voice distortion. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned Mitnica during your testimony. Could you please explain the term. What does the term denote?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I remember Mitnica as a child. I don't know how to explain the word "Mitnica" to you. Do you know what Mitnica is? It was like a border crossing. That's what "Mitnica" stands for. I wouldn't be able to answer your question precisely. This is the name that has been known for ages for that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that part of the town at the very entrance into Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether that part of the city was actually the last part of the city that the Yugoslav People's Army occupied during the operations around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I was in the hospital. I can't tell you. I was in no position to know whether it was the first one or the last one. I don't know. I can't answer that because I was in the hospital all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not hear that even later?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: No, I did not. But I think that it was among the first -- that there were negotiations with the army and the international community and Pilip Karaula and Zdravko Komsic, who were the commanders of Mitnica, they negotiated a surrender on a condition that civilians wouldn't be touched. They surrendered their weapons, but they made it conditional on the civilians being protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that was immediately before the arrival of the troops at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 37 of today's transcript, you said, inter alia, that you knew that you would be leaving Vukovar when the JNA arrived. That's on page 37 of today's transcript. In paragraph 26 of your statement it says the same.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 24 of your statement, to the sentence where you say: "Later I heard that Major Sljivancanin said that the hospital staff could stay and continue working. Most of the Serb personnel decided to stay." You stated earlier today that Major Sljivancanin said that only Serbs could stay.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I may have misspoken, only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard that?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: No. I was the last one to leave. I don't know whether you read

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Sljivancanin had already held a meeting with the medical staff when the auxiliary services had already been separated from the rest of the hospital staff, and I mean clerks, drivers, and others, they were the ones who were taken to the buses that unfortunately ended up at Ovcara. And the load included slightly wounded patients. Somebody came to tell us that we were the last to leave. We didn't know what was going on. Then I saw Mr. Sljivancanin in a meeting. And then we were taken out. There were three to four soldiers in a gauntlet on each side. They searched us. They were probably looking for weapons or I don't know what. And then we were loaded onto buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, could we get a redaction page 50, line 5, the location where the witness worked. In general, the fact that he worked at the hospital I don't think is problematic, but the specific location within the hospital, we tried to draw that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, when asking the -- let's -- sorry, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was it said in the morning at the meeting that you didn't attend and those who attended the meeting passed that message on to you?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 39 of today's transcript - you don't have that on the screen but it doesn't matter - you stated that there were two MUP members bearing the same name, Ivan, and in your statement you mention one of them.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Actually, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you mention both of them, but one of them was also known as Specijalac?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: You misunderstood me, I apologise. There were two Ivans who were MUP members and they secured the old hospital building. The third guy called Ivan, Ivan Bozak, was at the gate. He was our doorman. He was a hospital employee. The first two were not hospital employees. They were MUP members who provided security for the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, if you know, of course, why was this person's nickname special?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: May I? Yes, I may. I don't know. There was a special school. That means that he was a bit retarded, that he was not like anybody else. That's why we called him Specijalac. That's why he could work at the gate as doorman and he worked together with Bogdan Kuzmic, who allegedly ended up killing him. They were both porters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 40 of the transcript you said that you knew, or rather, assumed that these people would be executed, those who were singled out. Could you explain why didn't it occur to you that they could be sent to prison?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Because when we were taken to the barracks by those buses, paramilitaries, Arkan's men, Seselj's men, and the real army met us, although there were less actual army troops. And there were also high-ranking officers. I don't know whether it was Mrksic and Radic. I think they were there but not Sljivancanin. And they went around with knives and threatened us, telling us that they would slit our throats. They told one of our colleagues that they would rape his wife, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? One of the officers was reading from a list the names of people who were to be returned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. I mean, I assume -- I don't know what kind of rank he had but it was a high rank. He went around the buses because a list was made at the hospital. Dr. Ivankovic had asked Sljivancanin's permission to make a list of employees of the hospital from supporting services, specifying that these people had no weapons, et cetera, and they should be returned. However, not everybody from that list was returned because the fifth column in the hospital - that's my opinion - deleted some names because I know that my wife put certain names on that list and those people were deleted. They were not called out at the barracks, which means that the list was shortened in the hospital itself. It's not the same list that Dr. Ivankovic received in order to convey to Sljivancanin. I don't know if you understood me. If necessary, I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify one more thing. You said you went to Velepromet once a week to get supplies?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, all that has to be redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said at several points in your statement -- you mention the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Arkan's men, Seselj's men, and also members of the Yugoslav People's Army. I noticed there is no reference in your statement to reservists. Do you know that in the operations around Vukovar, the Yugoslav People's Army used not only the conscripts doing their regular military service but also recruits of older age groups that were recruited from the reserve force, the so-called reservists?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the Registrar tells me that we have some problems with the fact that you answer too fast while the microphone is still open. That causes problems because then we have to redact everything. So if you could please make a pause before you start answering the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll be more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, generally speaking, that in the Yugoslav People's Army, not only during the Vukovar operation but always, there were people who had already done their military service and then received a war-time assignment in the event of war or military drills?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I knew that before the war they called up reservists from time to time, but I was not thinking about that in the context of this war because, honestly, I never did my military service - I was declared unfit - so I didn't give it any thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then it is probably difficult for you to distinguish the uniform of reservists from the uniforms of others who belonged to what you called paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Probably. This is the first time I actually hear this suggestion. I had never given any thought to reservists, but I know that they were JNA because they looked like real soldiers. They were properly dressed in uniform, clean-shaven, whereas the others were unkempt and unshaven and looked any which way. The soldiers were better in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to your statement. Look at paragraph 35 of your statement. You said, among other things, that between 9.00 and 10.00 a.m., one of the medical assistants told you to go to the main entrance to the ER and going down the hallway you noticed that the patients who used to be in the hallway were missing. Does it mean that they had already been taken out of the hospital, put on buses, or taken in some other way?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Those more lightly wounded had been taken away, whereas those with serious injuries had already put -- been put on ambulances that went with us, with the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at the time when you were going out, was the convoy with the lightly injured still there or had it already left?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Because I was in that convoy with those five/six buses because they had been put on buses and regrettably they ended up in Ovcara, those lightly wounded. They were first taken to the barracks, and after the reading out of this list, some of us were returned, which was no guarantee that we would be released. Serb employees of the hospital first had to guarantee for us that we also worked for the hospital and did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, at that time you were not put in the convoy with other hospital employees but with the lightly injured?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: supporting staff, all of them were taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. 60 -- page 56, line 13 and 14, I'd say 15 also to be redacted, please. And, Mr. Witness, to make the business with the microphones work, because I noticed that it still doesn't, could I ask you after each question of Mr. Zivanovic to count in your head to five and then start answering. By that time, the microphone will be off and the interpreters will have finished their translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I'm sorry, I have no experience with this. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I see the time. Would this be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, we will take our second break of the day and come back at 12.45. We go into closed session now and the court usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Witness, may I remind you to count to five before answering. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let us just repeat. After leaving the hospital, you got on a bus where there were both employees of the hospital and people lightly injured. Were there also on the same bus members of the Croatian Home Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, but with your leave, Your Honours, I would like to clear up about the reservists. At the barracks there was not a single reservist because all of them were young and half of them were men from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Reservists are usually men who are mobilised in extraordinary situations such as an immediate threat of war or war time. Do you know that such mobilisations were also carried out in the territory of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't think so. I believe that they self-organised. Just as Croats organised themselves to defend Vukovar, the Serbs organised themselves as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to that bus. Could you tell us in your estimate what time was it when you got on the bus?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Well, between 10.00 and 11.00. I can't tell you exactly. It was 20 years ago, but it was between 10.00 and 11.00 because we had just distributed breakfasts and we from the kitchen were the last to come and we were put on the bus in a group. Everybody else was already on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that those buses ended up at the barracks in Vukovar. Tell me, approximately how much time did it take you to get to the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: About 20 minutes. If everything had been normal, we would have gotten there sooner, but since Vukovar was destroyed, streets were covered in debris, piles of debris, and those were not regular buses. They were military buses with those wooden seats and they moved slowly. It was difficult to move through all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that when the buses arrived at the barracks, there were people around the buses threatening those on the bus, and among those people there were also officers who did nothing to stop the others. I'd like to know, in your estimate, were those officers able to prevent that if they had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Of course they were able to. They just didn't want to. You see, if somebody is a high-ranking officer, they had some authority. But they just let it happen. When that bus was put together, when the group was put together to be returned, they made us go through a gauntlet and they were hitting us with bats, with clubs. And there was an officer there, a high-ranking officer, who didn't lift a finger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. In paragraph 45 of your statement you said that a JNA officer got onto one of the buses at one point, and when he got on the bus everybody went quiet. When you said "quiet," do you also mean the people around the buses -- look up that paragraph if you will.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I understand your question. I didn't mean that the crowd outside suddenly went silent, but those on the bus because they were waiting to see whom he would call out. And he also looked for Dr. Emedi, Dr. Farkas, Dr. Kucjanovic [phoen], journalist Esterajher, and some other people. Some prominent people from Vukovar, he wanted us to tell him whether we knew where those people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you also mentioned Sinisa Glavasevic among them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). He was lightly wounded somewhere around his ear or his nose. That was the last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will have to redact a few lines there in 60, 5, 6, 7, and 8, or something or thereabouts, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether that officer was also looking for Sinisa among the others?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: He did not look for Sinisa Glavasevic, just the other people I mentioned. They were all in the same profession except for Mr. Esterajher, who was a reporter for the Vukovar Radio. All the others were doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 46 I see that in addition to all these other names you also mention Sinisa Glavasevic. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Perhaps. You see, that was 20 years ago. It could be an error, but it's possible also that he was looking for him too. I'm certain about the others but I'm no longer certain about Sinisa Glavasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long did you stay at the barracks? How long did the bus you were on stay at the barracks and how long was it before you moved to the other bus?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: About half an hour, no more than 45 minutes, because as soon as we arrived that crowd gathered who threatened us with knives, et cetera. Then this official came, or officer, Mrksic, Radic, I can't remember who it was because I didn't know these people then. He called out names. It was very quiet. And everyone would move as soon as they got called out to the other buses. And the troops made a gauntlet. They had pieces of wood, clubs, metal pipes, et cetera, and they hit us with whatever they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 51 of your statement you mentioned that from the bus in which you arrived a total of 25 people got out. You say that some others remained on the bus and you give us their names. Now, let's clear this up. These people whom you name, are those the ones who stayed or the ones who moved with you to the other bus?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: When we got there with that list from the hospital, we were not sure, as I said before, that we were going to be released. We thought that Serb employees of the hospital would have to guarantee for us that we didn't have any weapons, whereas those people who remained, there were two employees of the hospital, Marko Vlaho and Mirko Vlaho, and the rest were not employees of the hospital. Marko Vlaho and the other man, I have a mind freeze now, those two men named Vlaho, they were employees of the hospital. But when the war began, since we had Serb drivers who left their jobs, needed to be replaced and they came. And nobody could give guarantees for them because the other staff of the hospital could not provide guarantees for them. That's why they stayed behind and they ended up at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have just spoken at cross-purposes. I meant the events at the barracks because I believe that paragraph 51 of your statement refers to that. You can take a look. And that's the time when you arrived to the barracks on the buses and you were transferred onto a different bus. I believe that that's where you were transferred to a different bus, a total of 25 people who would later on be returned to the hospital. I'm interested in the names that you mentioned in paragraph 51. Did those people remain on the bus that brought you to the barracks or were they transferred together with you to the other bus that would return to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: I apologise. I was looking at the transcript and I was not listening to you. Can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 51 of your statement. You say that a total of 25 people were taken off the bus. You're talking about the bus that arrived from the Vukovar Hospital and it reached the barracks and you were among those 25 people. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: No, you did not. There were around 25 people who were taken from all the buses and put onto one bus. We were taken to the hospital. The Serbian staff of the hospital had to provide guarantees that we had not been carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in paragraph 51 you mentioned the names of the people. Did those people remain on the bus from which you were taken out?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Jozo Adzaga remained, Miroslav Vlaho, and the other Vlaho whose first name was Mato. And let's see who else. Another man whom I didn't know, I didn't know his name, I know that he had worked at the Jugopetrol company before the war and that when he was on the bus together with us, when we reached the hospital he was accused of having killed Jovo Rakica, who was a well-known tradesman in Vukovar, and he was among those who were then taken back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will no longer insist on any further explanations. You mentioned a name [as interpreted] whose nickname was Bulidza. That's in paragraph 54 of your statement. Was he on the bus which took you from the barracks to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes. That Bulidza was a staff member at the hospital before the war. He was a butcher in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now could you please tell us something about -- you said in paragraphs 55 through 63. You described the return to the Vukovar Hospital, the journey to the hospital itself. And in paragraph 57 you mention Major Sljivancanin. Was he there when the bus arrived from the barracks to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was in the hospital all that time, for as long as the convoy did not depart. He was the person in charge. He was the one who said: This one can go.
