If somebody guaranteed for a certain person, then he would be let out from the bus and allowed to go to Ivo Lola Ribar Street, where the buses were forming the convoy. There were some ten ambulances, or perhaps even 15 ambulances, that transferred seriously wounded. There was staff members there. I don't know how many buses were there. I joined them at the end of the day. There was also the International Red Cross there and the international community escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the time of day when the separation took place, when people were separated into two different convoys, the one that stayed behind and then, I suppose, was taken towards Ovcara and the other that you joined? What was the time of day when that separation into two convoys took place?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: We were returned -- you asked me about the time when we left. That was between 10.00 and 11.00. We stayed there around half an hour, up to 45 minutes, then we returned. Some individuals got off. Sljivancanin would approve who could leave, who could not, based on guarantees, and that may have taken no longer than an hour. Then we crossed to the other side, to Ivo Lola Ribar Street, but the convoy did not depart straight away. I don't know what it was waiting for. It probably departed perhaps an hour to an hour and a half after all of those developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're now talking about the convoy that you joined, the convoy that would later go to Sremska Mitrovica; right?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: Could you see what was going on with the other convoy in which some people stayed, did it depart about the same time you did or earlier?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: No, we could not see them because we were on a different side of the street and we were on a different side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing that I would like to clarify and it concerns the shelling that I already asked you about, that was one of my first questions. Could you please tell me, how long did shelling last? How many days, how many weeks or months? You spoke about the shelling of the hospital and you said about 2.000 shells fell on the hospital on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: That was in the month of August. I don't know on what date it started and it lasted until the fall of Vukovar. It was uninterrupted. During the night it was not so frequent. From 11.00 in the evening until 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning shells did not fall so frequently. During the day they were falling on the hospital non-stop, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to do my math. It arises from that that about 180.000 shells fell on the hospital. If something like that had happened, I don't know what would have remained of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Sir, you misunderstood me. Even if shells were falling in the centre of the city we could hear it in the hospital. Thousands upon thousands of shells fell on the hospital and in the entire city. That shelling was intermittent, it did not stop. It was constant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I may have not understood you properly. I thought that you said that 2.000 shells fell on the hospital every day. It seems that you had in mind the entire city, but it did have an impact on the hospital. Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that at least a thousand shells fell on the hospital every day. In general terms, Vukovar was shelled for three months without any interruptions, with some breaks from 11.00 in the evening until 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning when shells did not fall constantly, although they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: A couple of questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, firstly, at transcript page 53, line 16, you mentioned a term "fifth column," this is on the transcript. Could you describe who were the fifth column and what that term means when you use it?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: In the hospital those were Serb staff members. We shared whatever we had, cigarettes and everything else. And when Vukovar and the hospital fell, then those people, individuals of Serb ethnicity, pointed their fingers at certain other staff members. They pointed them to Captain Sasa and Major Sljivancanin and laid accusations against them for God knows what.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Second question: In relation to these people, the Vlahos, in paragraph 32 of your statement you referred to a Marko Vlaho and you say he survived and lives in Zagreb. Then at paragraph 58 you refer to a Miroslav Vlaho and Mato, M-a-t-o, Vlaho, and you say that they stayed on the bus at the hospital when you got off the bus. So I'm trying to establish, because on the transcript before it wasn't entirely clear whether there were two or three Vlahos.

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: There were three persons by the same name. Marko Vlaho was the oldest, he was Miroslav Vlaho's father. The other Vlaho - what was his name? - was the oldest Vlaho's nephew. They were both drivers. Marko Vlaho was the driver who was taken out on the night when Captain Sasa entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, the way you phrased the question at 67, 8, you say: "In relation to these people ..." When I go to the previous question I would think that this is about those Serb people referred to as the fifth column, but I think they are Croats, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Indeed. That was not my intention to link it to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And that was my final question on re-direct. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question for you. I'm referring to the transcript page 62, mainly page 62. You spoke about the buses who took the hospital staff from the Vukovar Hospital to the barracks - that's the word in English, I believe. And 25 people from your bus returned from the barracks to the hospital because, according to you, according to your testimony, there were some Serb employees who could guarantee that those people, I believe that they were Croats, had not been carrying weapons. My question is this: Are you saying that the only reason why a Croat member of hospital staff was taken to the barracks and then from there was returned to the hospital was a guarantee provided by a Serb member of hospital staff that that Croat had not been carrying arms? Is that the only reason? Was there any other reason?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Partly. I don't think that you understood me properly. First of all, those were hospital staff members who were returned because Major Sljivancanin received a list, and those were not all people from my bus. They were gathered from all of the buses. There were five or six buses. The high-ranking military officer called our names and we came from all the buses, some 25 or 30 of us. And then when we arrived in front of the hospital, then our colleagues, local Serbs, had to guarantee that we had not been carrying arms. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thank you. Can we say that, for example, if a Croat had a Serb wife that guarantees were understood? Was it automatic? Could a Serbian wife guarantee that her Croatian husband did not carry arms?

utterances.speaker: GH-103
utterances.text: Yes, it was automatic. If the wife guaranteed for him, he would be set free. But there were also Serbian doctors. For example, a pharmacist provided guarantees for me and for my brother. She was a Serb and she guaranteed for the two [as interpreted] of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you for your clarifications regarding guarantees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noted just one error in transcript. The witness said that three persons, the pharmacist guarantees for three persons, not for two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you mention three persons? Did you mention three persons, Mr. Witness? Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bosnic, who was the head of our hospital pharmacy, was a Serb. We were on very good terms. We

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). She guaranteed for the three of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry about that, but this will have to be redacted. I should have asked for private session. If that is all -- Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just a quick technical matter to hopefully help with the -- with the associated exhibits there was a video-clip and the 65 ter number should be 4798.2. It was not one that we saw in court today, but it was associated with the statement. And also, there is a list uploaded in e-court which links the numbers of the coloured photos that are easier to see with the black and white photos which are attached to the statement, and we've put that as 3258.2. And so if they could be admitted along with the statements, I believe it would assist when it comes to analysing this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Isn't that a rather complicated way of getting this straight, Mr. Gillett? Wouldn't it be easier if you would tender again the statement with coloured photos annexed to it rather than make all these loops?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We thought this was the easiest way to proceed because when the statement was taken, he signed copies that were in black and white, and these colour photographs are from the previous proceeding and easier to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So ordered. Mr. Witness, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you very much for your assistance. You are now released as a witness, and once in closed session, the court usher will escort you out of court. Thank you very much. We wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.
